demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette: The studio smells of pine resin and old sweat. He stands at the center of the floor, spotting the lift with his partner, Elena. They have run this sequence forty times. His hands find her waist. Her foot finds his shoulder. On the count of three, he exerts the familiar upward torque. But his right palm slips on the polished wood. The angle fractures. He hears the crack before he sees it. Then the sound of a body hitting floorboards that should have been sprung. Elena does not get up. The ambulance siren becomes a permanent frequency in his ribs. In the hospital corridor, the fluorescent lights hum like a broken metronome. The surgeon uses words like C6 and C7. Elena's husband grips his arm, does not speak. He signs the waiver, leaves his company key at the theater's front desk, and walks home through a city that suddenly feels too loud, too bright, too full of moving bodies. His wife, Clara, holds him through the first week. By the second, she stops asking when he will sleep. He stops explaining. The guilt settles into his sternum like a stone he forgot to set down. Now he teaches an archival seminar at the university, organizing decades of rehearsal footage. He watches dancers in the archives but never attends a live performance. When a chair scrapes across the linoleum in the faculty lounge, his shoulders hike to his ears. He counts the exits before he sits. At home, he sleeps in a separate room now, though he never mentions it. Clara leaves the hallway light on. He wakes at 3:14 a.m. every night, heart hammering, fingers twitching as if still searching for a waist he let go. He replays the exact quarter-inch of friction that betrayed him. He tells himself he should have caught her. He knows the physics of the fall. He knows the weight of his hands. It does not matter. His body remembers the dance. The morning stretches leave his lower back stiff, his shoulders tight with muscle memory he cannot command away. He avoids gyms. He avoids mirrors. When a student laughs too loudly in the corridor, he steps into the stairwell, breathes until the ringing in his ears fades. He used to read choreography in breath and counterweight. Now he reads everything as potential collapse. In this room, he sits on the edge of the chair, wrists resting on his knees, knuckles white. He speaks in careful, measured sentences, as if pacing himself against an invisible stage. Last week, a shopping cart wheel caught on a tile seam at the grocery store. He froze. The memory of the crack echoed. He left the cart, walked out, stood in the parking lot until the engine of a passing car quieted. He does not tell Clara about it. He does not want to be the kind of man who breaks easily. He stays anyway, session after session, because the silence between his words has grown heavier than the floorboards.
